Alive when you are: changing, growing, learning, moving.
Dead when you are: unchallenged, inactive, uninterested, passionless.

Alive is when there is electrical transmission across the brain stem.

Dead is the termination of electrical signal across the brain stem.

There are only a few things that actually cause death.

  1. The dissociation of the brain stem, such as guillotine severing the head or a projectile scattering the brain stem material.

  2. Creating a hostile environment for electrical signals, such as a heart attack causing a buildup of CO2 in the blood.

  3. Necrosis of the brain stem itself.

  4. Ionizing radiation that disrupts electro-chemical signals between neurons.

  5. Chemical interference of the brain stem functioning.

  6. Brain parasites that eat the neuron tissue, such as Naegleria fowleri amoeba.

  7. Hemorrhaging that causes the brain to swell and crush the brain stem.

  8. Lack of blood supply to the brain stem that results in necrosis of the brain matter.

This is a good answer for things with central nervous systems. Let me take some small issue with it though.

Even when that ceases, won't much of your tissue continue living for some time? Of course. Why aren't you alive until all of your tissue dies? Perhaps you argue the brain stem is more essentially the entity than some other random lump of tissue. If that's so, why stop at the stem? If my forebrain got mangled such that everything that makes me me was lost, wouldn't I be dead even if some tissue kept on going?

Even if your argument is that the forebrain death still leaves something that can handle autonomic functions and live for a time, it would be incapable of providing itself with nourishment and the tissue would die quickly. Analogously, if the brain stem died, you'd no longer be able to breath, etc. and the tissue would end up dying after a (shorter time).

Finally, looking at the reverse, if you kept the forebrain intact and destroyed the brain stem, your consciousness would continue until the sort time it took for that tissue to die. In this time would you be a ghost? Your definition would say the person is dead but they're still conscious.

The problem here is that "you" is not an integrated whole. You're several interacting systems and different parts can die at different times. Our consciousness is probably the closest thing there is to a self, so it's reasonable to say that an individual has died when the tissue that supports that part of the brain has died.

I think your answer are more rules of thumb for things that will lead to total tissue death without intervention that is generally beyond medical science.
